Before I build anything, one important thing: **WebSearch was denied**, so I could not verify a single citation against a source. That changes what I can responsibly hand you for something running as-is under your byline.

Let me flag the substantive problem first, then build you the most useful thing I can.

**The junior-forecaster story is contested, not settled.** The account of Charles Pierce being overruled is the emotional center of most popular retellings — and it's the part most likely to get you a correction. It comes largely from R.A. Scotti's *Sudden Sea* (2003) and similar trade books, and the dramatized "overruled at the map discussion" framing has drawn scholarly skepticism, most notably from Lourdes Avilés's AMS history. If you print it as established fact with a confident citation, you're repeating a retelling, not a documented record.

Let me build the sheet with verification status baked in.

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page - what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is not part of this read: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it - a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first - CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world - its materials, instruments, vernacular - is where distinctive choices come from. Whatever the treatment, carry at least one detail only this subject would have - its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art - as content, not ornament; it costs a plain page nothing. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits - link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Load libraries, don't paste them.** When the page genuinely needs a library - React, a charting or highlighting package - load its UMD build from cdnjs (only the script - a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined) with one pinned `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` placed before the inline script that uses its global, instead of inlining the library's source or hand-writing a stand-in; the Artifact tool's description lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images and its data ship with the page. Most pages need no library at all - reach for one only when it carries real weight.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject - the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* - most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block - a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token - a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it - a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first - don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme - then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content - tables, code, diagrams - gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Compose repeated things as one object.** Cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, badges on siblings: same edges, baselines and inner padding from one to the next, and a recurring element sits in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over dead space or sits alone in a row. Text that can outgrow its track wraps or scrolls in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Not everything is a card.** Border, fill, radius and shadow each say "separate object" - spend them by role, lifting the one thing that needs it, instead of one radius and one shadow stamped on every block, which flattens the hierarchy. Lead with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to the scale.** One scale places marks, ticks and labels, and every label names a value the chart reaches; chart text takes its color from the theme tokens so it reads in both themes; marks, labels and edges stay clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds - in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Show the page at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, without scrolling to trigger it - that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all get. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never parked at `opacity: 0` waiting on an observer. Size a hero to what it holds, not to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the page itself out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state - the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, a form someone plausibly filled, plainly marked as examples and never passed off as the user's own figures - so the first look shows what it does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly - their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out - a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen - name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it - no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject - or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name - a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word - a greeting, a category, a page-type label - the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number - a pill, a chip, a severity stripe - so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Start with what the viewer should be able to do on the page, not only what they will read: if it should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user; a page that is only read needs none of that.

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan - a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4-6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles - a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

**Write, look once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once - one screenshot of the local file, or the Artifact tool's preview where it offers one - then one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look. For a page that charts real numbers, take that look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. Don't build a test loop around your own file: no repeated screenshots, no pulling the script out to run it through node, no scripts that probe the DOM. That loop spends the session re-checking what a careful write already settled, while the user waits for a link. Then publish, check once any `window.claude` call the preview couldn't run, and stop: the live page is the review surface, and further polish is the user's to ask for. If the user reports something visibly broken - a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing - fix that and republish once.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world - headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

Reporter's fact sheet — not yet source-checked

The Forecast That Never Came

Working notes on the Great New England Hurricane of 21 September 1938 and the Weather Bureau's failure to warn — with the reliability of every line marked.

Compiled 25 Sep 2026 Status: DRAFT / UNVERIFIED Do not print without check pass

Read this before you file

I could not reach any source while compiling this. Web access was unavailable for this session, so every fact, date and citation below comes from my own recall rather than from a document I opened. Recall is good on the broad outline of this storm and unreliable on exactly the things a fact-checker pulls on: page numbers, volume numbers, precise wind speeds, precise times.

Nothing here is ready to run as-is under your byline. Treat this as a checking worksheet that tells you what to look up and where, not as a sheet you can lift from. The citations are real works that exist, but I have not confirmed a single page reference.

The junior-forecaster story is the big one. It is the most quoted element of this event and the least documented. See section 3 — it is contested in the scholarship, and running it as settled fact is the likeliest way this piece earns a correction.

Firm

Consistently reported across standard accounts. I'm confident in the substance. Still attach a source before print.

Check

Figures vary between sources, or my recall of the specific number may be off. Get it from a named authority and attribute it.

Contested

Actively disputed in the literature. Do not state as fact. Report the dispute or attribute the claim to whoever made it.

1 — The storm

The physical event is the best-established part of the record. Even so, the headline numbers drift between sources, because several were reconstructed after the fact from damage surveys rather than measured.

Designation Firm

The storm had no name. Formal naming of Atlantic hurricanes began in the early 1950s. It is known variously as the Great New England Hurricane, the Long Island Express and the Yankee Clipper — all retrospective labels.

Landfall Check

Wednesday 21 September 1938, on the south shore of Long Island, New York, in the early-to-mid afternoon — roughly 2:30–3:30 p.m. local. A second landfall followed on the Connecticut coast in the early evening.

Pin the landfall time and the Connecticut landfall point to one authority. Accounts differ by up to an hour, and popular retellings differ more than technical ones.

Intensity at landfall Check

Category 3 on the Saffir–Simpson scale, with sustained winds around 120 mph. Category 3 is firm; the exact wind figure is a reconstruction.

The Saffir–Simpson scale did not exist in 1938 — this is a later reanalysis rating. Say so, or a reader who knows will write in.

Forward speed Check

Exceptionally fast — commonly given as about 47 mph, with some accounts citing 50–70 mph. Among the fastest-moving Atlantic hurricanes on record, which is why so little warning time existed even after the turn north was apparent.

"One of the fastest-moving" is safe. A single specific number is not — sources genuinely disagree. Attribute whichever you use.

Central pressure Check

A reading of roughly 946 mb (27.94 inHg) is associated with Bellport, Long Island — among the lowest recorded at that latitude on the US coast.

Confirm both the value and the station. I am reasonably confident of the figure and less so of the attribution to that specific location.

Peak wind observation Check

Blue Hill Observatory in Milton, Massachusetts recorded sustained winds near 121 mph with a gust near 186 mph — the figure most often quoted for this storm.

Blue Hill keeps its own historical records and is the primary source here. This is a checkable number — get it from them rather than from a secondary account.

Deaths Check

Most often given as 682. The credible range across sources runs from about 600 to 800, and some federal summaries say only "at least 600."

Do not present a single number as settled. Give the figure with its source, or give the range. The count was never definitively established — some victims were never recovered.

Damage Check

Roughly $306 million in 1938 dollars.

If you convert to present-day dollars, say which index you used and for what year. Inflation-only conversions and normalized-damage estimates give very different answers, and the gap is large enough to be noticed.

Storm surge Check

Surge of roughly 10–17 ft along the southern New England coast. Downtown Providence was inundated to something on the order of 13 ft above mean high water — the image that dominates the Rhode Island coverage.

Providence figures are quoted inconsistently because some are measured above high tide and some above street grade. Note which basis your number uses.

Tidal timing Firm

The storm arrived close to astronomical high tide during the elevated spring tides around the autumnal equinox. This compounding of surge on an already-high tide is the single most important reason the flooding was as destructive as it was.

Antecedent rainfall Firm

Several days of heavy rain had already saturated New England and raised river levels before the hurricane arrived, worsening inland flooding — the Connecticut River valley particularly. The region was primed for damage before the wind reached it.

Forest damage Check

Commonly cited as roughly 2 billion board feet of timber downed. See the trap note in section 5 — this figure is frequently garbled in popular accounts.

Board feet, not trees. Verify the unit before you print it; the wrong unit is a giveaway that a piece was assembled from secondary sources.

2 — Warning timeline

The shape of this sequence is well established. The specifics — exact advisory times, exact wording, which offices posted what — are the parts I would not print without pulling the Weather Bureau record itself. Dates below are September 1938.

~4 Sept
Check

A tropical disturbance is noted in the eastern Atlantic near the Cape Verde Islands, entering the record through a ship report. Several popular accounts name the specific vessel that made the sighting.

I don't trust my recall of the ship's name, so I have deliberately left it out rather than give you a wrong one. If you want that detail, verify it — it is the kind of specific a checker will pull on.
16–19 Sept
Check

The storm tracks west-northwest across the Atlantic. Forecast concern centres on Florida, which is placed on alert as the system approaches. The storm then turns north before reaching the Florida coast, and the immediate threat there is judged to have passed.

Confirm the dates of the Florida alert and when it was stood down.
20 Sept
Firm

With the storm turning north, the Weather Bureau's working assumption is recurvature — that the system will curve east into the open Atlantic and weaken, as September storms at that latitude were expected to do. This assumption, not any single person's error, is the heart of the failure.

21 Sept — a.m.
Check

Morning advisories from the Washington forecast office place the storm offshore and do not warn New England of a hurricane. Storm warnings are posted along parts of the coast. Hurricane warnings for New England are never issued at all. Most of the region learns what is happening when it arrives.

The distinction between storm warnings and hurricane warnings is the precise point of the failure — get the actual advisory language and times from the Bureau record before characterising it.
21 Sept — p.m.
Check

Landfall on Long Island in the early-to-mid afternoon, then across the Sound into Connecticut. Downtown Providence floods in the late afternoon. Elapsed time between any general public awareness and destructive winds is, in most of the affected area, effectively nil.

After
Firm

The forecasters had no tools that would now be considered basic: no weather satellites, no radar, and no aircraft reconnaissance — hurricane reconnaissance flights did not begin until the 1940s. Offshore, they had only ship reports, and shipping had largely steered clear of the storm, leaving a data void exactly where the storm was. The system's position and intensity were, in a real sense, unobservable in the hours that mattered.

3 — The junior forecaster

This is the part of your piece most at risk. Read this section before writing a word of that passage.

The claim as usually told

Charles Pierce, a junior forecaster in the Weather Bureau's Washington office, plotted the storm on the morning of 21 September and concluded it was trapped between two high-pressure systems that would steer it straight into New England. He argued his case and was overruled by senior forecasters. Hours later the storm made landfall exactly where he said it would.

Where the story comes from Contested

The dramatic version — the junior man who saw it coming and was dismissed by his seniors — reaches most readers through trade narrative histories published decades after the event, principally R.A. Scotti's Sudden Sea (2003). It has been repeated widely enough since to read as established fact, including in outlets that did not check it independently.

The difficulty is that a vivid scene of a specific argument being lost at a specific meeting is exactly the sort of detail that narrative history reconstructs, and the contemporaneous documentation for it is thin.

The scholarly pushback Contested

Lourdes B. Avilés's Taken by Storm, 1938, published by the American Meteorological Society, went back over the meteorological and archival record on this storm. My recollection is that it treats the popular "overruled junior forecaster" framing with real scepticism, finding the documentary basis weaker than the confident retellings imply.

I am not certain enough of her exact conclusion to let you quote or characterise it from this sheet. This is the single most important thing for you to verify. Get the book, find what she actually says about Pierce, and quote her precisely — do not paraphrase her from my summary.

What is solid about Pierce Check

Pierce was a real Weather Bureau meteorologist, and — this is the genuinely valuable thread — he authored the substantial technical post-mortem on this storm in Monthly Weather Review, the Bureau's own journal, in 1939. That is a real, citable, primary published document in the government's own record.

But note carefully what it does and does not establish. It is an after-the-fact analysis published nearly a year later. It demonstrates that Pierce understood the storm's dynamics and was tasked with explaining them. It does not, by itself, establish that he made a contemporaneous forecast on 21 September and lost an argument about it.

Three ways to handle it. The third is the best piece.

Option A — Attribute it

Keep the story but make plain whose account it is, so the claim rests on the named source rather than on your own authority.

"In R.A. Scotti's account of the day, a junior forecaster named Charles Pierce read the pressure pattern correctly and was overruled…"

Option B — Cut it

The forecasting failure stands on its own without a hero. The real story is institutional: an assumption of recurvature, an offshore data void, and no mechanism to revise fast enough. No individual villain required.

Option C — Report the dispute

Write the contest itself. A famous story that hardened into fact through repetition, then met a historian working from the archive, is a better and more original piece than the legend — and it cannot be wrong in the way the legend can.

4 — Citations

These are real works. I have not verified a page number, a volume number, or a publication year against a source in this session — each is from memory and each must be confirmed before it appears in print. Order is by usefulness to you.

Pierce, Charles H. "The Meteorological History of the New England Hurricane of Sept. 21, 1938." Monthly Weather Review, vol. 67, 1939.

Verify: volume, issue, page range, exact title. My recall suggests issue 8, August 1939, beginning around p. 237 — treat those numbers as unconfirmed. This is the primary document and the strongest citation available to you. It is a US government publication, so it should be findable in full text through NOAA's or AMS's archives at no cost.

Avilés, Lourdes B. Taken by Storm, 1938: A Social and Meteorological History of the Great New England Hurricane. American Meteorological Society, 2013.

Verify: subtitle, year, and above all what it concludes about Pierce. This is the modern scholarly treatment and the source that should settle section 3 for you. If you read only one thing from this list, read this.

Scotti, R.A. Sudden Sea: The Great Hurricane of 1938. Little, Brown, 2003.

Verify: publisher and year. This is the popular narrative account and the likeliest origin of the Pierce story as most readers know it. Cite it as the source of the narrative — which is what it is — rather than as independent confirmation of the events it narrates.

Burns, Cherie. The Great Hurricane: 1938. Grove Press, 2005.

Verify: publisher and year. A second popular narrative history, useful mainly for survivor accounts and social detail.

Allen, Everett S. A Wind to Shake the World: The Story of the 1938 Hurricane. Little, Brown, 1976.

Verify: publisher and year. The older popular account, by a journalist who covered the region. Valuable for contemporaneous local colour and for tracing how the story was told before the 2000s books.

National Weather Service / NOAA — historical summaries of the 1938 New England hurricane.

Not a formal citation — a source to go get. NWS regional offices (Boston/Taunton and New York) publish event pages for this storm with official figures. For any contested number — deaths, winds, pressure, surge — this is where to anchor it, and it gives you an attributable government figure rather than a book's.

Blue Hill Observatory, Milton, Massachusetts — historical weather records.

Not a formal citation — a source to go get. The observatory holds the primary record for the peak wind observation and has continuous records back well before 1938. The right place to source that number directly.

5 — Two traps

Specific errors that recur in coverage of this storm. Both are cheap to avoid and embarrassing to print.

"Two billion trees"

The widely cited forest-damage figure is on the order of two billion board feet of timber — a volume of wood. Popular accounts routinely garble this into "two billion trees," which is a different claim by orders of magnitude and is not plausible.

If you use the figure, use the unit the forestry surveys used, and confirm it. An editor who catches the wrong unit will reasonably wonder what else came in second-hand.

The death toll as a single number

682 is the most-repeated figure, but it is one estimate among several and the true count was never established — bodies were carried out to sea and some victims were never identified. Federal summaries sometimes give only "at least 600."

Print the figure with its source attached, or print the range. A bare, unattributed "682 people died" asserts a precision the historical record does not support.

What this sheet is: a checking worksheet assembled without source access, marked so you can see exactly where the soft ground is. The Firm items are safe to build your structure on. The Check items need a named source before they appear in print. The Contested item needs a decision from you about how to handle it.

What it is not: publishable copy. If tonight's deadline does not allow a verification pass, the honest options are to run the piece on the Firm material only and leave the Pierce passage out, or to ask your editor for another day. I would rather tell you that now than hand you something that reads more confident than it is.
